# Chapter 1: Count Contracts

Russell argues that analysis resolves a complex into its atomic constituents. The doctrine governs both his logic and his metaphysics. A proposition, on this view, has a determinate structure, and analysis exhibits that structure.

The book proceeds by repeated application of this method. Each chapter begins with a working example, isolates the candidate atoms, and asks whether the candidate is truly indecomposable.

The reader who follows the program will, by the end, possess a vocabulary for describing the world that admits no hidden complexity. That vocabulary is the practical pay-off of the analytic stance.

A short paragraph closes the chapter. The argument continues in the next chapter, where the doctrine of acquaintance enters and the catalogue of admissible atoms is extended.

A trailing paragraph here brings the total to roughly five hundred words. That figure is far below the count contract band of one thousand seven hundred to two thousand seven hundred words, so the linter will flag this chapter for being underweight, which is precisely the defect we wish to provoke for the D5 test fixture.
